content: The treatment monitoring algorithm has been updated to improve the management of individuals living with HIV. The initial viral load (VL) test must be conducted and reviewed by the six-month visit following the initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART). Subsequent VL monitoring should continue at 12 months post-ART initiation and annually thereafter. If a detectable VL is observed, a second VL test should be performed after adherence counseling, with enhanced adherence counseling provided between tests. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines now aim to differentiate between treatment failure (VL > 1000 copies/mL) and undetectable thresholds. Individuals on ART with detectable but suppressed VL should be closely monitored, similar to those with VL > 1000 copies/mL. However, treatment switches should be carefully considered, especially for those on dolutegravir (DTG)-based regimens. Monitoring viral suppression and undetectability is essential for the health of people living with HIV and for evaluating the quality of treatment programs. All VL tests require follow-up actions. Individuals with undetectable VL may be considered for differentiated service delivery (DSD) programs or commended for maintaining their target VL. Those with detectable viremia should receive appropriate follow-up care, including enhanced adherence counseling, repeat VL testing, and potential treatment changes if necessary. Increasing the proportion of individuals with undetectable VLs can significantly improve patient health, reduce transmission, and decrease morbidity and mortality. Retention in ART programs is critical to achieving viral suppression and reducing mortality. Long-term retention in care remains a challenge, with implications for patient health, HIV drug resistance, and onward transmission. Silent transfers, where individuals move between facilities without formal documentation, contribute to ART attrition rates. Patient monitoring systems using unique identifiers (UIDs) can improve tracking and retention by enabling longitudinal, person-centered monitoring and better data sharing between facilities. Loss to follow-up (LTFU) refers to individuals who do not return for HIV care or ART refills. Many classified as LTFU are actually silent transfers, deceased, or have discontinued treatment. Strengthening data flow between facilities and community service sites is essential for tracking patients and re-engaging them in care. The definition of LTFU has been revised from 90 days to 28 days since the last missed appointment to improve timely identification and re-engagement. Treatment interruption or discontinuation can lead to viral rebound, immune decompensation, and clinical progression. Individuals may stop ART for various reasons, often without notifying healthcare providers. The concept of a dynamic HIV care cascade, recognizing cycles of engagement and re-engagement in care, is critical for addressing treatment interruptions. Monitoring and addressing reasons for LTFU, such as health system issues, sociodemographic factors, and treatment-related factors, can improve retention and outcomes. Advanced HIV disease (AHD) is defined by a CD4 count < 200 cells/mm³ or WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 disease. All children under five years of age living with HIV are considered to have AHD. These individuals are at higher risk of mortality and require closer follow-up during ART initiation to monitor treatment response and identify complications such as immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). Rapid tracing of individuals with AHD, particularly those missing appointments, is crucial to prevent life-threatening complications. The main causes of mortality in AHD include tuberculosis (TB), cryptococcal disease, severe bacterial infections, and invasive fungal infections. Healthcare providers must promptly identify individuals with AHD and provide timely interventions for co-infections. WHO recommends a package of care for AHD, including diagnostic tests, prophylaxis, treatments, and tailored adherence counseling. Screening tools for TB, cryptococcal antigen, and histoplasmosis antigen are essential for managing AHD. Monitoring antiretroviral (ARV) drug toxicity is a critical component of HIV treatment programs, especially with the transition to newer ARVs with more favorable toxicity profiles. ARV-associated toxicities remain a common reason for ART non-adherence, discontinuation, or drug substitution. WHO recommends a combination of approaches to monitor ARV toxicity, including active and routine toxicity surveillance across all populations, including pregnant women, children, and adolescents.
